concept.name: Kubernetes Workloads & Services

relationships.description: Connects Kubernetes Workloads & Services to canary deployments in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Kubernetes separates compute lifecycle (Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job) from stable network routing (Service + EndpointSlice + kube-proxy/eBPF) using declarative label-selector reconciliation.
spark.keyTakeaway: Match the workload controller to statefulness and scheduling needs, and pair readiness probes with PodDisruptionBudgets so zero-downtime rollouts never route traffic to unready or terminating pods.

concept.whyItMatters: Running stateless APIs in a StatefulSet wastes operational simplicity, while running Kafka or PostgreSQL in a Deployment risks split-brain storage corruption. Understanding how controllers reconcile Pods and how Services decouple ephemeral Pod IPs via EndpointSlices and kube-proxy is what separates resilient production clusters from cascading rollout outages and 502 storms.
whenToUse: Deployment: stateless HTTP/gRPC services, workers, and frontends needing rolling updates (`maxSurge`/`maxUnavailable`) and instant horizontal scaling.
StatefulSet: distributed databases (PostgreSQL, Kafka, etcd, Redis) requiring stable DNS (`pod-0.svc`), ordered startup/teardown, and persistent per-pod PVCs (`volumeClaimTemplates`).
DaemonSet & Job/CronJob: node-level agents (Fluent Bit, Cilium, Prometheus node-exporter) on every node, or finite batch/scheduled tasks with `backoffLimit` and `ttlSecondsAfterFinished`.
whenNotToUse: Bare Pods without a controller—if a node dies, a standalone Pod is never rescheduled.
StatefulSet for stateless workloads just to get predictable pod names—ordered scaling slows down HPA bursts and complicates node drains.
Default `ClusterIP` Service for gRPC or client-side load-balanced databases—use a Headless Service (`clusterIP: None`) so clients discover all Pod IPs directly via DNS.
keyPoints: Controller specialization: Deployments manage ReplicaSets for interchangeable pods; StatefulSets bind each ordinal (`-0`, `-1`) to its own PersistentVolumeClaim and DNS entry `<pod>.<headless-svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local`.

Service abstraction: Services match Pods via label selectors and maintain `EndpointSlice` objects (default max 100 endpoints per slice) that `kube-proxy` (iptables/IPVS) or eBPF (Cilium) programs into kernel packet-forwarding rules.

Zero-downtime termination race: `kubelet` sends `SIGTERM` to the Pod concurrently with the Endpoints controller removing the Pod IP from `EndpointSlices`; a `preStop` sleep (5–10s) prevents in-flight 502s while iptables/eBPF rules propagate.

Probe separation: `startupProbe` protects slow-booting JVMs/ML models, `readinessProbe` gates Service traffic inclusion, and `livenessProbe` restarts wedged containers—never point `livenessProbe` at downstream DB health.
Voluntary disruption safety: PodDisruptionBudgets (`minAvailable` or `maxUnavailable`) block `kubectl drain` and cluster autoscaler evictions from taking down quorum or all replicas simultaneously.

examples.title: Zero-Downtime gRPC Rollout with Headless Service & PreStop
examples.scenario: A Go gRPC payment service experiences 0.8% HTTP/2 503 errors during every Deployment rollout because kube-proxy iptables updates lag behind Pod SIGTERM.
examples.outcome: Adding a `lifecycle.preStop` hook (`sleep 10`) inside the 30s `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` window plus a `readinessProbe` lets EndpointSlice removal finish across all 40 nodes before the gRPC server stops accepting connections, dropping rollout errors to 0%.

examples.title: 3-Node Raft/Kafka Cluster on StatefulSet
examples.scenario: A messaging team needs 3 Kafka brokers with dedicated 2 TB NVMe PVCs and fixed peer hostnames that survive node replacements.
examples.outcome: Using a StatefulSet with `serviceName: kafka-headless` (`clusterIP: None`) and `volumeClaimTemplates` guarantees `kafka-0` always reattaches to `data-kafka-0` and resolves at `kafka-0.kafka-headless.prod.svc.cluster.local`.

tradeOffs.factor: iptables vs. IPVS vs. eBPF (Cilium) kube-proxy mode
tradeOffs.pro: IPVS and eBPF use O(1) hash-table lookups, keeping service-routing latency flat even past 10,000 Services.
tradeOffs.con: Default `iptables` evaluates rules sequentially in O(N), causing noticeable rule-sync CPU spikes and packet latency above ~5,000 Services.

tradeOffs.factor: ClusterIP Load Balancing vs. Headless Service (`clusterIP: None`)
tradeOffs.pro: ClusterIP gives a single virtual IP (VIP) with transparent L4 round-robin for HTTP/1.1 clients.
tradeOffs.con: L4 VIPs pin long-lived HTTP/2 or gRPC TCP connections to one backend Pod; Headless Services expose all Pod IPs in DNS A/AAAA records for client-side L7 balancing.

tradeOffs.pro: OrderedReady starts `0 → 1 → 2` sequentially, ensuring primary election or seed discovery completes safely.
tradeOffs.con: In a 50-shard cluster, OrderedReady can take 20+ minutes to scale or restart; `Parallel` launches all ordinals simultaneously when the app handles peer discovery.

failureModes.name: Liveness Probe Cascading Restart Storm
failureModes.description: A `livenessProbe` checks a downstream database; when the DB blips for 10s, Kubernetes kills and restarts all healthy API pods simultaneously, amplifying recovery load.
failureModes.mitigation: Check downstream dependencies only in `readinessProbe` (to shed traffic) and keep `livenessProbe` strictly local (process/event-loop responsiveness).

failureModes.name: PDB Deadlock Blocking Node Upgrades
failureModes.description: A `PodDisruptionBudget` sets `minAvailable: 100%` or `maxUnavailable: 0`, preventing `kubectl drain` and Managed Node Group upgrades from ever completing.
failureModes.mitigation: Always leave at least 1 disruption budget (e.g., `maxUnavailable: 1` or `minAvailable: 2` on a 3-replica set) and monitor PDB `disruptionsAllowed`.

failureModes.name: SIGTERM / EndpointSlice Propagation Race (502s)
failureModes.description: A Pod exits immediately on `SIGTERM` in 50 ms, before `kube-proxy` finishes removing its IP from iptables on all worker nodes, causing clients to hit a dead socket.
failureModes.mitigation: Add a `preStop: exec: command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 10"]` hook and ensure `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` exceeds `preStop + in-flight drain`.

failureModes.name: StatefulSet Stuck Terminating on Lost Node
failureModes.description: A worker node crashes hard; Kubernetes refuses to recreate `pod-0` elsewhere because at-most-one semantics forbid two `pod-0` instances sharing one PVC.
failureModes.mitigation: Verify the old node is fenced/dead (e.g., via Cloud Controller Manager) before force-deleting the stuck Pod (`--grace-period=0 --force`).

commonMistakes: Omitting `resources.requests` and `limits`, causing pods to land in `BestEffort` QoS and get OOMKilled first during node memory pressure.
Using `latest` image tags without `imagePullPolicy: Always` or immutable SHA digests, leading to version drift across nodes.
Setting `readinessProbe` and `livenessProbe` with identical tight timeouts on a slow-starting app without a `startupProbe`, trapping pods in `CrashLoopBackOff`.
Assuming deleting a `StatefulSet` deletes its `PersistentVolumeClaims`—PVCs intentionally persist (`persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy`) and must be cleaned up explicitly if ephemeral.
Exposing internal microservices with `type: LoadBalancer` instead of `ClusterIP` + an Ingress/Gateway API controller, creating unnecessary public cloud LBs and cost.

sections.content:
## The idea

Kubernetes separates **what runs** (Workload Controllers) from **how it is reached** (Services). Controllers continuously watch the API server and reconcile desired state (`spec.replicas`, `template`, `volumeClaimTemplates`) against live Pods. Because Pods are mortal and receive new IPs on every reschedule, a `Service` acts as a stable virtual abstraction: it selects matching Pods by labels, writes their IPs into `EndpointSlice` objects, and programs kernel forwarding rules (`iptables`, `IPVS`, or `eBPF`) across every node.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a `Deployment` rolling update (`maxSurge: 1`, `maxUnavailable: 0`) on a 3-replica API behind a `ClusterIP` Service:
1. **Surge**: Updating the container image creates a new `ReplicaSet` and scales it to 1 Pod (`4` total Pods).
2. **Gate**: `kubelet` runs `startupProbe` and `readinessProbe`. Until `readinessProbe` returns `200 OK`, the Pod's IP is marked `ready: false` in the `EndpointSlice` and receives zero traffic.
3. **Shift**: Once ready, `kube-proxy` adds the new Pod IP to the Service's forwarding rules, and the old `ReplicaSet` scales down by 1.
4. **Drain**: The terminating Pod receives `SIGTERM`, runs its `preStop` `sleep 10` while `EndpointSlice` removal propagates across nodes, finishes active HTTP requests within `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30`, and exits cleanly.

sections.content:
## Workload Controllers & Service Types

- **Deployment**: Stateless pods; supports `Recreate` or `RollingUpdate` and instant `kubectl rollout undo` via `revisionHistoryLimit` (default 10).
- **StatefulSet**: Ordered `0..N-1` identity, stable headless DNS, and sticky PVCs.
- **DaemonSet**: Exactly one pod per matching node (taints/tolerations control master/GPU scheduling).
- **Job / CronJob**: Finite completion (`completions`, `parallelism`, `backoffLimit: 6`); CronJobs enforce `concurrencyPolicy` (`Allow`, `Forbid`, `Replace`).
- **Service Types**: `ClusterIP` (internal VIP), `Headless` (`clusterIP: None`, raw DNS), `NodePort` (`30000–32767`), and `LoadBalancer` (cloud NLB/ALB).

## Workload Controller Comparison

| Controller | Pod Identity | Storage Binding | Scaling & Update Order | Typical Use Case |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Deployment** | Random hash suffix | Shared RWX or ephemeral | Parallel (`maxSurge` / `maxUnavailable`) | Stateless REST/gRPC APIs, consumers |
| **StatefulSet** | Fixed ordinal (`-0`, `-1`) | Dedicated RWO PVC per ordinal | Ordered `0→N` (or `Parallel`) | Kafka, PostgreSQL, etcd, Redis Cluster |
| **DaemonSet** | Per-node hash | `hostPath` / node-local | RollingUpdate (`maxUnavailable`) | Log collectors, CNI, GPU device plugins |
| **Job / CronJob** | Completion-scoped | Ephemeral / batch PVC | `parallelism` workers until `completions` | DB migrations, nightly Spark/ETL runs |

## Failure modes

1. **gRPC Pinning on ClusterIP**: HTTP/2 multiplexes all RPCs over one TCP connection; `kube-proxy` only load-balances at TCP `SYN` time, pinning 100% of traffic to one Pod until a Headless Service or L7 Envoy mesh is used.
2. **OOMKill Cascade**: Missing memory `requests == limits` (`Guaranteed` QoS) lets noisy neighbors trigger node eviction.
3. **Ingress / Service Selector Mismatch**: A typo in `spec.selector` leaves `EndpointSlices` empty (`0` endpoints), returning immediate `connection refused`.
4. **Probe Timeout Thrashing**: Under CPU throttling (too-tight `resources.limits.cpu`), `livenessProbe` misses its 1s timeout and restarts healthy Pods.

## Traffic Shifting & Graceful Shutdown

In production, pair `Deployment` rollouts with `PodDisruptionBudget` (`maxUnavailable: 1` or `25%`) and `topologySpreadConstraints` (`maxSkew: 1` across `topology.kubernetes.io/zone`) so an entire Availability Zone failure or node drain never drops capacity below quorum. For high-RPS services, remove `limits.cpu` (or set it generously) while keeping `requests.cpu` accurate to avoid CFS quota throttling during traffic bursts.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Define `startupProbe`, `readinessProbe`, and local-only `livenessProbe` on every long-running container.
- [ ] Add a `preStop` sleep (5–10s) and align `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (>30s) with app drain time.
- [ ] Attach a `PodDisruptionBudget` to every multi-replica Deployment and StatefulSet.
- [ ] Set `requests` for CPU/memory and pin container images by immutable SHA256 digest.
- [ ] Use a Headless Service (`clusterIP: None`) or L7 proxy for gRPC/HTTP2 workloads to avoid TCP connection pinning.

interviewProblems.title: Kubernetes Workloads & Services
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Kubernetes Workloads & Services. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Kubernetes separates compute lifecycle (Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job) from stable network routing (Service + EndpointSlice + kube-proxy/eBPF) using declarative label-selector reconciliation.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Service & EndpointSlice applies the primary invariant and coordinates with kube-proxy / eBPF.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, kube-proxy / eBPF experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Check downstream dependencies only in `readinessProbe` (to shed traffic) and keep `livenessProbe` strictly local (process/event-loop responsiveness).

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Match the workload controller to statefulness and scheduling needs, and pair readiness probes with PodDisruptionBudgets so zero-downtime rollouts never route traffic to unready or terminating pods.
Avoid trap: Omitting `resources.requests` and `limits`, causing pods to land in `BestEffort` QoS and get OOMKilled first during node memory pressure.
Avoid trap: Using `latest` image tags without `imagePullPolicy: Always` or immutable SHA digests, leading to version drift across nodes.
When to reach for it: Deployment: stateless HTTP/gRPC services, workers, and frontends needing rolling updates (`maxSurge`/`maxUnavailable`) and instant horizontal scaling.

When to reach for it: StatefulSet: distributed databases (PostgreSQL, Kafka, etcd, Redis) requiring stable DNS (`pod-0.svc`), ordered startup/teardown, and persistent per-pod PVCs (`volumeClaimTemplates`).

putItTogether.title: Putting Kubernetes Workloads Together
putItTogether.summary: Match the workload controller to statefulness and scheduling needs, and pair readiness probes with PodDisruptionBudgets so zero-downtime rollouts never route traffic to unready or terminating pods.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Kubernetes Workloads before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Adding a `lifecycle.preStop` hook (`sleep 10`) inside the 30s `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` window plus a `readinessProbe` lets EndpointSlice removal finish across all 40 nodes before the gRPC server stops accepting connections, dropping rollout errors to 0%.
